properties are the consumer's responsibility. every reference resolves through the bag (subjects) or through `properties`. there is no out-of-band authority. every undefined or `null` input fails closed. purpose **why.** a pure-logic library cannot enforce trust on its inputs. the boundary must be drawn explicitly so consumers know what they own. confusion at the boundary is the most common cause of access-control vulnerabilities. **how.** the library trusts every value in the bag. the consumer builds the bag from trusted sources (verified session, db rows) and never from request-supplied data. any reference the engine cannot resolve — missing subject, missing field, undefined operation input — fails closed. **why this way.** moving trust into the library would force product knowledge into it: where do credentials come from, how is a session validated, what counts as authoritative. keeping the library logic-only and the boundary explicit lets the engine stay reusable while making the consumer's security responsibility unambiguous. **what.** the trust model of the engine — what the library guarantees, what the consumer is responsible for, and how the boundary is drawn. reference  examples use the same fictional document-management product as dsl-rules (`dsl-rules.md`): workspaces contain folders, folders contain documents, users may belong to teams. reference › the trust boundary a bag built from request-supplied data (cookies treated as truth without verification, json body fields used as identity, jwt claims that weren't validated) is architecture list-query  list-query contributor shared/libs/list-query  design decisions for `@prowd/list-query`. read this before changing the public surface. scope types shared be ↔ fe sort-string grammar + parser zod schema factory (be) drizzle orderby + pagination helpers (be) urlsearchparams serializer (fe) it does **not** own: http error rendering (the app's existing zod → 400 path handles it) caching or query-key helpers for tanstack query cursor pagination sql-level `nulls first/last` customisation (we use postgresql defaults) translation of filter objects beyond the pagination/sort/search triplet plus flat key-value extras the lib owns the mechanism of the pagination + sort + search contract end-to-end: dependency direction **the config imports lib types only.** per the architecture rule (*configs → module public types, and lib types only when not module-mediated*). pagination defaults are not module-mediated — the module doesn't wrap the lib. **module validators** import from both and pass defaults explicitly. this keeps the factory pure (no ambient config lookup) and makes the defaults visible at every call site. consumer validators (configs/<module>/api/*.api.ts)
        │
        ├──→ @configs/list-query           (product defaults)
        │         │
        │         └──→ @prowd/list-query   (lib types)
        │
        └──→ @prowd/list-query             (createlistqueryschema, types)

consumer repositories ──→ @prowd/list-query/server  (drizzle helpers)
consumer fe adapter   ──→ @prowd/list-query/client  (url serializer) **the lib never imports from configs, modules, or apps.** it ships baseline constants so it's standalone and fully unit-testable in isolation. the config is thin — it re-exports those baselines as the product-tunable values and adds nothing else today. three-tier default fallback  list_query_baseline (lib)
    → list_query_defaults (product config, typical)
         → per-call-site override (rare, justified) call sites normally pass `list_query_defaults`. overriding on a specific endpoint is permitted when there's a genuine reason (e.g. a heavy join page where 25 rows is too many) but should come with a comment explaining why. two entry points, not three `.`        — isomorphic (types, sort parser, constants) `./server` — be only (zod factory, drizzle helpers) `./client` — fe only (url serializer) finer splits (`./zod`, `./drizzle`) were considered and rejected. a be file already knows it can use both zod and drizzle; pushing users to import from `/zod` and `/drizzle` separately adds ceremony without catching any realistic mistake. `/server` + `/client` is the coarsest split that still prevents the one mistake worth preventing: a fe bundle accidentally pulling in drizzle. splits: no envelope executor the helper can't actually enforce the invariant — the two queries are built separately and the helper only receives the result of each builder chain. it would be enforcement theatre. the 2-line `promise.all([listq, countq])` is not worth wrapping. the code-review rule ("one named `whereexpr` variable, passed to both queries") is more visible in the diff than a helper that hides the shape. the primitive helpers (`buildorderby`, `applypagination`) plus disciplined review are cleaner than an executor pretending to guarantee something it can't. an early design considered `executelistquery({ db, list, count })` that would take two query builders and enforce "same where" at the type level. we dropped it: sort grammar choice rejected alternatives: `sort=type:asc,name:desc` — more verbose, no real advantage `sort[]=type&sort[]=-name` — spec says a single `sort` field, not array params json in query string — hideous in urls, hostile to url-building tools the `-` prefix is conventional (github, stripe, many rest apis) and the resulting strings are compact and easy to read. comma-separated, `-` prefix for descending: sort=type,-name,createdat tiebreaker behaviour ties on a secondary column still exist beyond the tiebreaker, but they're impossible to observe if the tiebreaker is a primary key. total ordering is guaranteed. the tiebreaker is auto-appended by `buildorderby` so call sites can't forget it. when a caller's declared sort already includes the tiebreaker column (by column reference identity), we honour their declared direction and don't duplicate the column in the order by. this matters for endpoints like "sort by id desc to show newest first" — the caller explicitly wants desc and should get it. null ordering it matches postgresql's built-in behaviour overriding would force every call site to think about it the contract promises "postgresql defaults" — explicit, documented, predictable if a future endpoint needs different null ordering, add it to `buildorderby` as an option at that time. not before. postgresql defaults: nulls last on asc, nulls first on desc. we don't emit `nulls first/last` because: why co-located tests  matches `availability-check`'s style. architecture §12 permits either co-located `*.test.ts` or a `__test__/` folder; co-located makes atomic refactors (moving a helper + its test in one diff) straightforward and keeps the test physically next to the code it covers. `scoped-ac` uses `__test__/` for historical reasons and a different module structure; neither is wrong. why a thin config package  `configs/libs/list-query/` today exports only `list_query_defaults`. it's not overbuilt because pagination defaults are the only product tunable. if future pagination policy ever needs more (e.g. per-endpoint override maps, per-product maximum), it lives in this same folder — the structure is already there. unreviewed unreviewed unreviewed

sort syntax list-query  list-query contributor shared/libs/list-query  canonical grammar for the `sort` query param. grammar a leading `-` on a field means descending. no prefix means ascending. fields are comma-separated. whitespace around tokens is trimmed; whitespace inside an identifier is invalid. sort     := field ("," field)*
field    := ["-"] identifier
identifier := [a-za-z_][a-za-z0-9_]* examples  ascii | input | parsed |
|---|---|
| `name` | `[{name, asc}]` |
| `-createdat` | `[{createdat, desc}]` |
| `type,-name,createdat` | `[{type, asc}, {name, desc}, {createdat, asc}]` |
| `  name  ` (trimmed) | `[{name, asc}]` |
| `type, -name , createdat` (inner whitespace trimmed) | `[{type, asc}, {name, desc}, {createdat, asc}]` | rejections (all → 400 at the validator)  ascii | input | reason |
|---|---|
| `bogus` (not in whitelist) | `unknown_field` |
| `name,-name` (same field twice) | `duplicate_field` |
| `name,` (trailing comma) | `empty_token` |
| `,name` (leading comma) | `empty_token` |
| `name$` (bad char) | `invalid_character` |
| `-` (bare minus, field becomes empty) | `invalid_character` | why this grammar **comma-separated** — widely used, easy to type in urls, copy-pastable. **`-` prefix for desc** — convention in github api, stripe api, json:api, many others. zero ceremony compared to `:asc` / `:desc` suffixes. **duplicate fields rejected, not collapsed** — the client is stating a contradiction (`name` asc and `name` desc). silently collapsing would hide a bug. **empty tokens rejected** — a trailing comma is almost always a bug in url construction. never silent. **identifier-only fields** — the whitelist is the real guard, but rejecting weird characters early produces clearer errors and stops sql injection attempts dead before they reach drizzle. parser behaviour multiple errors are collected in one parse — if the client sends `sort=nope,alsonope`, both fields produce errors so the validator can report both at once. the parser (`parsesortstring`) never throws. it returns a discriminated result: type parsesortresult =
  | { ok: true;  value: sortspec[] }
  | { ok: false; errors: parsesorterror[] }; ts adding a field to an endpoint's whitelist add it to `sortable` in the endpoint's `createlistqueryschema({...})` call. add its drizzle column to the `columnmap` passed to `buildorderby` in the repository. add a test case asserting the new field sorts correctly. the two lists (zod whitelist + repo column map) **must** stay in sync. a field in `sortable` but missing from `columnmap` is a runtime error (thrown by `buildorderby`). a column in the map but missing from `sortable` is dead code — the validator will reject it at 400 before it reaches the repo. deliberately not supported `asc` / `desc` suffixes (e.g. `name:asc`) — use the `-` prefix. per-field null ordering (`nulls first/last`) — postgresql defaults only. array parameter syntax (`sort[]=...`) — a single comma-separated `sort` field only. nested field paths (`organization.name`) — flat identifiers only. endpoints that join tables pick stable per-endpoint aliases and add them to `sortable`. unreviewed unreviewed unreviewed

mapr: the documentation standard docs  docs  each thing is documented in one canonical place, nothing is duplicated. documentation is positional: a doc lives at the scaffolding level it governs and applies to everything below it; navigation points to it. every doc follows the same structure, so a reader always knows where to look. the structure runs axiom principles → purpose → reference detail. by reading the axiom principles you should understand the architecture principles and no reference should drift from axioms. documentation of reusable domains (example: shared libs and seed slices) separates **consumer** (how to use) from **contributor** (how to change). agents write verbose, drifting prose by default, and no human can re-read every doc on every change. mapr fixes the shape so the constraints are impossible to miss because every doc leads with its what and why before the how. artifacts mapr stands for map → axioms → purpose → reference. three artifacts, one job each. **map**: navigate. pointers only, never teaches. it is a `map.json`. **doc**: the canonical reference. axioms → purpose → reference. it is a `<id>.json` in a folder of its own. **adr**: record one past decision. context → decision → consequences. it is an `adr.json`. a map that teaches, a doc that records history, or an adr in a canonical doc are all violations. doc structure axioms, then purpose, then reference, in that order. **axioms**: plain sentences. one universal invariant per line, most abstract first, most concrete after. easy to read, no long prose, no subjectiveness, no method names or shapes. if it is a mechanism, it is reference, not an axiom. **purpose**: one paragraph, plain dev voice. state why the decisions were made. do not define universal concepts, do not restate the axioms. someone reading the axioms might understand the rules but the purpose of those rules might not be self evident: that is the role of the purpose. **reference**: all concrete rules and mechanics that are relevant, still plain dev voice and with diagrams over prose. **cross-cutting rationale** is stated once, in the constitution, and referenced. never repeated per doc. the shape of a doc <id>/<id>.json {
  "id": "<id>",
  "type": "doc",
  "title": "title",
  "axioms": [ { "text": "numbered sentences, one idea each, abstract to concrete" } ],
  "purpose": { "intro": "one paragraph: why these decisions exist" },
  "reference": [ { "topic": "…", "claims": [ … ] } ]
} map structure a map is navigation only. the central map is the registry (`docs/engine/registry.ts`): domain entry points only, one per location. a local map (`<location>/docs/map.json`) points to everything inside that context, nothing outside it. an entry is a pointer and a one-liner: id, title, path, kind and summary, plus its status. a map starts with instructions for whoever reads it. a map of a reusable domain points to `consumer/` and `contributor/` docs, then `adr/` and `glossary/`. nothing else. a reusable domain shared/libs/<name>/docs/ map.json          ← local map
glossary/         ← the terms
consumer/         ← usage docs (how to use)
contributor/      ← internal docs (how to change)
adr/              ← decisions a location that is not a reusable domain apps/main/docs/ map.json          ← local map
glossary/         ← the terms
<doc>/            ← the docs, flat
adr/              ← decisions consumer and contributor the split applies to reusable domains. libraries and seed slices are reusable domains: their docs split into `consumer/` and `contributor/`. the root, main, the apps and infra are not reusable domains: their docs stay flat, with no consumer and no contributor. adr structure an adr records one past decision. an entry has a date, a title, a context, a decision and consequences, and it is append-only. a decision that stops being true is superseded by a new entry, never rewritten. the adr is stored in `adr/`, beside the docs it concerns. glossary every location has its own glossary. terms are written inline as `[[term]]` or `[[term|shown text]]`. a term can be used across locations: the viewer reads every glossary at runtime. map and adr locations a map and an adr sit with the docs they concern. global: the registry and the root's `adr/`. seed slice: `<slice>/docs/map.json` and `<slice>/docs/adr/`. lib: `shared/libs/<name>/docs/map.json` and `…/docs/adr/`. app: `apps/<name>/docs/map.json` and `…/docs/adr/`. maintenance loop the order is fixed: axioms approved before reference, never the reverse. draft the axioms, or the change needed. human approves. write from scratch, or scan the reference for gaps and clashes. report gaps and clashes to the human. human approves the resolution. update the reference. human approves the reference. update the history in `adr/` if it is an architectural change. compliance each file and folder of the registry is labelled mapper compliant or not. a doc is compliant when its id is its folder and file name, it has axioms, a purpose and a reference, and it sits where its location's rules say. a location is compliant when it has a map, an `adr/` and a `glossary/`, and every file under its docs is in the map or is an asset. markdown left in a location is not compliant: it waits in `.old-markdown-to-sunset`. unreviewed unreviewed unreviewed

architecture ui  ui contributor shared/libs/ui  only the architect may modify this document. fundamental principle  **absolute, hermetic separation between structure and appearance.** ascii | concern | owns | lives in |
|---------|------|----------|
| **markup** | positioning, flow, semantic identity, flags | components, layouts, pages |
| **theme** | every visual property: color, border, radius, shadow, spacing, typography, transitions, opacity, cursor, effects | one theme object per product | visual primitives  everything rendered on screen is one of five primitives: ascii | primitive | what | morphological families |
|-----------|------|----------------------|
| **rectangle** | bounded region with boundary + interior | surface, overlay, control, control group, field, list, layout |
| **vector graphic** | icons, svgs, logos, decorative shapes | shape |
| **media** | images, video, embedded content | media |
| **typography** | styled text | not a family (see below) |
| **animation** | transitions, keyframes, motion | cross-cutting — applied via tokens | morphological families  every visual element belongs to one family. all share the same base token shape (**surfacecontainertokens**). some extend it. the element → family map is `shared/libs/ui/types/elements.ts`, one line per element, and it also says which elements have `sizes` (scale). the theme types, the engine and the components derive from it. ascii | # | family | attribute | prefix | examples |
|---|--------|-----------|--------|----------|
| 1 | surface container | `element` | `surface` | card, panel, section, header, footer, badge, avatar, tile, alert, separator, panel-header, panel-content, panel-footer, progress, spinner, skeleton |
| 2 | elevated overlay | `element` | `overlay` | dialog, drawer, panel-overlay, popover, tooltip, toast, hamburger-menu |
| 3 | interactive control | `element` | `control` | button, icon-button, chip, toggle, switch, checkbox, radio, tab-trigger |
| 4 | interactive control group | `element` | `control-group` | topbar, navbar, sidebar-nav, tab-bar, breadcrumb, pagination-bar, button-group, toggle-group |
| 5 | field | `element` | `field` | input, textarea, select, combobox, date-picker, otp |
| 6 | list container | `element` | `list` | table, list, accordion, menu, tree-view |
| 7 | shape | `element` | `shape` | icon, svg, logo, decorative |
| 8 | media | `element` | `media` | image, video, embedded |
| 9 | layout | `layout` | — | shell, shell-side-nav, shell-top-nav, shell-none, page, page-header, second-page-header, page-body, left-sidebar, main, main-header, second-main-header, main-body, container, context-panel, right-sidebar, scroll-area | morphological families › family-specific extensions  ascii | family | extra tokens beyond surfacecontainertokens |
|--------|---------------------------------------------|
| elevated overlay | scrimcolor, scrimopacity, scrimblur, entrance/exit animation |
| field | placeholdercolor, placeholderopacity, obfuscation, caretcolor |
| list container | row, cell, separator, alternating (each partialsurfacetokens) |
| media | objectfit, aspectratio, overlay, filter |
| layout | (no extensions — uses surfacecontainertokens directly) | morphological families › two attributes: `element` and `layout` `element` = morphological identity (what this surface is) `layout` = structural region (where this sits in the page) both are themed identically by the cascade engine. the separation exists because they are different concerns: layout is the frame, element is the surface inside it. a dom node carries **either** `element` or `layout`, never both. morphological families › part attribute `part="name"` marks a structural sub-region inside a themed ancestor. it goes on plain divs that need designer-controlled spacing, gap, or background without carrying a full element identity. only parts explicitly declared in the theme's `parts` field for that surface produce any css — undeclared parts are invisible to the engine. a node never carries both `part` and `element`/`layout`. not implemented in the engine today; the engine knows only its own zones, `data-part="start-icon" | "end-icon" | "thumb" | "scrim"`. the universal shape: surfacecontainertokens every property is optional. only define what you customize. every family uses the same base token structure: boundary         border (width, style, color, per-side), radius (all, per-corner),
                 effect (named preset or layers), outline (width, style, color, offset)

interior         background, backgroundalpha, foreground, opacity,
                 padding (all, x/y, per-side), gap (all, h/v),
                 separator, scrollbar (thumb, track, width)

defaulttypography  typographytype (pointer to root scale), texttransform,
                   textdecoration, texteffect

tint             accent color (for emphasis/status composition)
cursor           css cursor value
smartbleed       false | 'normal' | 'rounded' | 'border' | 'border-rounded'
transition       duration, timing

states           hover, active, focus, selected, disabled, loading
status           neutral, error, warning, success, info, destructive
emphasis         hero, primary, secondary, tertiary, quiet typography **default typography (on surfaces):** surfaces that contain text use `defaulttypography` to point at a root type scale. changes per size variant. color comes from `interior.foreground`, never from typography. **typography in markup:** multiple text styles inside a container use `element="type--heading2"`, `element="type--bodysmall"` etc. **18 root type scales:** heading1–4, bodyextralarge–bodyextrasmall, quotelarge–quotesmall, code, numbersextralarge–numbersextrasmall. typography is **not a family**. handled two ways: the cascade  a designer builds incrementally. each level only declares what it changes: ascii | level | what | selector |
|-------|------|----------|
| l1 | primitives | `:root` vars |
| l1b | modes + derivations | `:root` / `[data-mode]` vars |
| l2 | family defaults | `[element^="{prefix}--"]` or `[layout="..."]` |
| l3 | element overrides | `[element="{prefix}--{name}"]` |
| l4 | concept overrides | `[concept="x"] [element="..."]` |
| l5 | contextual overrides | `[element="a"] [element="b"]` | the cascade › overlay axes (compose with any level)  ascii | priority | axis | values |
|----------|------|--------|
| 3 (highest) | state | hover, active, focus, selected, disabled, loading |
| 2 | status | neutral, info, success, warning, error, destructive |
| 1 (lowest) | emphasis | hero, primary, secondary, tertiary, quiet | priority is the author's: the engine emits the `combined` entries of a surface in the order they are written. write emphasis first, then status, then state, if that is the priority you want. the cascade › scale (structural, not an overlay)  `scale` adjusts padding, typography, icon size. never colors. values: xs, sm, md, lg, xl. only elements with `sizes: true` in the elements table can be authored per scale; the engine emits `[element=…][scale=…]` from an element's `sizes`, never at family level, never inherited from a parent. the cascade › concepts concepts work identically for elements and layouts. product-specific semantic identity. a concept wraps elements and overrides their visual treatment. grouped by concept in the theme: concepts: {
  knowledge: {
    card: { accent: 'brand-2', ... }
  },
  dashboard: {
    maincontent: { interior: { background: 'gray-50' } }
  }
} typescript tint mechanism emphasis defines a **pattern** (filled, outlined, ghost) and sets `tint` status overrides `tint` to recolor the pattern properties reference `'tint'` or `'smart-bw'` — they adapt automatically primary button: `tint='brand-1'`, `bg='tint'`, `fg='smart-bw'` → blue filled. primary + error: status overrides `tint` to red → red filled, same pattern. **smart-bw:** auto-picks black or white based on resolved background lightness. prevents combinatorial explosion of emphasis + status combinations. smart bleed  a theme-driven mechanism where a child element extends its background into the parent's padding/border area. resolved at build time — the engine computes the parent's padding/radius from the cascade and emits concrete negative margins. ascii | value | behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `false` | off |
| `'normal'` | bleeds over padding, outer corners rounded, inner edges straight |

mobile design: why the library is shaped this way ui  ui shared/libs/ui   what changed, and why this repo is a seed for many products, each with its own themes. that condition holds, so the choice is reversed: **one vocabulary.** `emphasis`, `status`, `scale`, `state`, read from `ui/types/axes.ts`. the translation files are gone: there is nothing to translate. **one law.** `ui/types/elements.ts` says which elements exist, on which platform, with which axis values. a mobile component's props are typed from its row. **one theme type.** a mobile theme is a `mobiletheme` (`ui/types/theme.ts`): the same primitives, families, elements and cascade as a web theme, without what only the web has, with what only a phone has. **the theme owns the look.** a component holds structure and behaviour; every visual value comes from the theme through `useelement`. the first version of this library, taken from the llc project, chose react native's usual vocabulary (`variant`, `tone`, `size`), a hand-written theme of its own, and kept a file per component translating its props to the web's. its own design note said when to revisit: when a second theme or several brands are on the roadmap. how a theme reaches a component  themes/<id>/v<n>/theme.ts          a mobiletheme, authored
        │   mobile/theme-engine     (pnpm theme:build:mobile)
        ▼
themes/<id>/v<n>/generated/<id>.native.json
        │   themeprovider
        ▼
useelement("button", { emphasis, status, scale, states })  →  { view, text, color, icon } the web engine turns a theme into css and the browser resolves the cascade. react native has no cascade, so the mobile engine emits each rule as a *fragment*, in the order the cascade applies them, and `resolve` (in `src/theme/resolve.ts`) keeps the fragments whose axes match and merges them. the colour composition (tint, background alpha, `smart-bw`) is the web stylesheet's formula, computed in javascript. what a component still owns **accessibility.** role, state, label. a component without it is not done. **native props.** a component wraps a react native component and passes its props through. **press feedback per platform.** ios dims (`theme.press.opacitydim`), android ripples (`theme.press.ripple`); both come from the theme. the `active` state restyles the element on both. **structure.** row or column, what goes where. never a colour, a size or a spacing. what react native cannot do, and what stands in  ascii | the web has | mobile does |
|---|---|
| the cascade | fragments, resolved by `useelement` |
| `:hover` | nothing. `long-pressed` is the state for what a held press reveals |
| inherited text colour | a component passes its text style to its own text |
| a stylesheet swapped at run time | a new `theme` or `mode` on the provider re-renders its consumers | not there yet concepts, contextual overrides and rules (theme levels 4 to 6) are not emitted: they need a component's ancestry at run time. gradients, text effects and blur are not emitted. the engine lists what it skipped in the output's `unsupported`, and prints it. the unit tests of the first version tested the old props and were removed with them. this repo has no test runner for react native yet; the tests are owed. unreviewed unreviewed unreviewed

`@libs/mobile-components` ui  ui shared/libs/ui  the mobile ui library: react native components on the same contract as `@libs/web-components`. the rationale is in `design.md` (`./design.md`). the contract a mobile component is one element of that table. it has the same name as its web twin and the same axis props: `emphasis`, `status`, `scale`, `state`. its first line says which element it is and which web component, at which version, it mirrors. the code is not shared. the web component renders html and is styled by css; this one renders react native views and reads its style from the native theme. one table rules both libraries: `shared/libs/ui/types/elements.ts`. each row is an element, with its family, the platforms it exists on, and the values it takes on each axis. quick start  import { themeprovider, button, card, badge, text } from "@libs/mobile-components";
import { stack } from "@libs/mobile-layouts";
import theme from "<themes>/bounx-mobile/v1/generated/bounx-mobile.native.json";

<themeprovider theme={theme} mode="light">
  <card>
    <stack dir="row" align="center" justify="between" gap={12}>
      <stack gap={4} size="fill">
        <badge>group session</badge>
        <text type="heading4">junior squad</text>
      </stack>
      <button scale="sm">start</button>
    </stack>
  </card>
</themeprovider> tsx components every interactive component sets its accessibility role and state, and passes the native props of the react native component it wraps. ascii | component | element | web twin |
|---|---|---|
| `button` | `control--button` | button |
| `card`, `cardheader`, `cardcontent`, `cardfooter` | `surface--card`, `--header`, `--content`, `--footer` | card and its regions |
| `badge` | `surface--badge` | badge |
| `avatar` | `surface--avatar` | avatar |
| `input` | `field--input` | input |
| `phoneinput` | `field--phone-input` | phoneinput |
| `field`, `label` | `surface--label`, `--field-description`, `--field-message` | label and the field wrappers |
| `choicegroup` | `control-group--choice-group` with `control--toggle` | the choice group |
| `group` | `surface--group` | a titled section |
| `emptystate` | `surface--empty-state` | emptystate |
| `icon` | `shape--icon` | icon, same semantic names, same icon set (lucide) |
| `text` | the typography levels, `type--<level>` | the `type--*` attribute |
| `stepper` | a composite of `button-group`, `button`, `button-group-text` | none: mobile's own | `stack` is in `@libs/mobile-layouts`. theme `themeprovider` takes a native theme (the `<id>.native.json` the mobile theme engine writes) and a colour mode. `useelement(element, axes)` returns the element's style for its axes: `{ view, text, color, icon, extras }`. `usepart(element, part, axes)` does the same for a surface inside an element (a list's row, a switch's thumb). `usetype(level)` and `usecolor(name)` read a typography level and a colour. a component never writes a colour, a size or a spacing of its own. a component is themed only by reading the theme. there is no cascade in react native. states  `active` (pressed), `focus`, `selected`, `disabled`, `loading` are shared with the web. `long-pressed` and `swiped` are mobile's. there is no `hover`. a component computes its states from what happens to it and also accepts `state` to force one. unreviewed unreviewed unreviewed
